title: 2024 concession speech
body:
On November 6, 2024, one day after losing the presidential election to [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]], Harris formally conceded the race in her first public remarks since Election Day, urging supporters to "accept the results" while adding that "while I concede this election, I do not concede the fight that fueled this campaign."[n] She delivered the speech at Howard University, her alma mater, where her campaign had held its election-night watch party; she had never addressed that crowd on Tuesday night as early optimism curdled after midnight.[n] Harris confirmed that she had spoken with the president-elect by telephone, pledged to aid a peaceful transition of power, and said she would never stop fighting for truth and justice.[n]

Badlands writer [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] observed that Harris "looked tired and disappointed" but had given "one of the most coherent speeches she's ever given," reading the authenticity of her disappointment as evidence that she had genuinely expected to win.[n] Ashe also noted that portions of the address echoed Trump's own rhetorical cadences — "never stop fighting," "the people are powerful" — and questioned who had written the remarks, while objecting to any Harris role in the transition.[n] Harris's instruction that supporters accept the outcome was echoed by Liz Cheney and Joy Behar, even as Democratic partisans online cycled visibly through denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance.[n] Ashe further pointed out that Harris had not gone through a primary, undercutting her standing to tell her own voters to "let it go" rather than demand audits.[n]

Harris's raw vote total, roughly 66 million, placed her near Barack Obama's 2012 result and Hillary Clinton's 2016 result, and far below the 81 million votes credited to [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]] in 2020 — a gap Badlands writers treated as evidence of an anomalous 2020 count rather than a Harris-specific collapse.[n]

title: 2024 election victory and its immediate aftermath
body:
Trump won the 2024 presidential election on November 5, 2024, taking both the Electoral College and the popular vote and sweeping the contested states of Georgia, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, with Arizona and Nevada projected to follow.[n] Decision Desk HQ projected his return to the White House, making him the first president to win non-consecutive terms since Grover Cleveland in 1892.[n] Republicans simultaneously recaptured the Senate for the first time in four years, while control of the House remained undecided the day after the election.[n] [[kamala-harris|Kamala Harris]] conceded on November 6.[n]

Commentators emphasized the scale of the comeback: Trump prevailed after being impeached and acquitted twice, indicted four times, surviving two assassination attempts and absorbing what Just the News described as an unparalleled avalanche of lawfare, media, Big Tech and Democratic opposition.[n] Beyond his personal vindication, the result was framed as a once-in-a-generation realignment deeper than 2016, as black men, Hispanic voters and young voters shifted toward him while Arab and Muslim voters underperformed for Harris — an exodus dubbed "D-Exit," the American analogue of [[brexit|Brexit]].[n]

Foreign reaction was immediate. Israeli Prime Minister [[benjamin-netanyahu|Benjamin Netanyahu]] was the first world leader to congratulate him, hailing "history's greatest comeback" and "a powerful recommitment to the great alliance between Israel and America."[n] Ukrainian President [[volodymyr-zelensky|Volodymyr Zelenskyy]], European Commission President [[ursula-von-der-leyen|Ursula von der Leyen]] and British Prime Minister [[keir-starmer|Keir Starmer]] followed with congratulations, while Moscow offered only guarded optimism.[n] Badlands writer [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] argued that legacy-media anxiety focused conspicuously on Western Europe and Israel rather than the United States itself, reading the globalist alarm as recognition that "the US is patient zero for the sovereign restoration."[n] [[ghostofbasedpatrickhenry|GhostofBasedPatrickHenry]] cast Trump and [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]] as co-captains of the [[sovereign-alliance|Sovereign Alliance]] and noted Trump's threat to impose tariffs marking up EU goods by 100–200 percent.[n]

On the domestic legal front, Justice Department officials moved to "wind down" the two federal criminal cases brought by special counsel [[jack-smith|Jack Smith]] before Inauguration Day, citing the post-Watergate policy against prosecuting a sitting president.[n] In the Middle East, the Yemeni [[houthis|Ansar Allah]] movement told Newsweek that Trump could spare the American economy further damage by reining in Israel's war in Gaza, while expressing doubt he would honor his promises to Arab voters.[n]

title: Reaction to the 2024 Trump election victory
body: On November 6, 2024, as the world absorbed news that [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] would return to the White House, Peskov delivered Moscow's first official reaction, stressing that US–Russia relations were already beyond further damage: "It is still almost impossible to worsen relations – they are at the lowest point in history."[n] Pressed on whether [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]] would issue a formal congratulatory message, Peskov said he was aware of no such plans but added "we will see," leaving the door open.[n] His tepid framing was paired with a more cautiously optimistic line from Foreign Ministry spokeswoman [[maria-zakharova|Maria Zakharova]], and together the two signaled a Kremlin wait-and-see posture.[n] Badlands writer [[ghostofbasedpatrickhenry|GhostofBasedPatrickHenry]] joked that Peskov "looks like he was sent straight from Central Casting to star as a Russian character in a 1980's action film," while conceding that his stern disposition was deserved.[n]

title: Reaction to the 2024 Trump election victory
body: Following [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s victory in the November 2024 US presidential election, Zakharova struck a notably warmer tone than Kremlin spokesman [[dmitry-peskov|Dmitry Peskov]], telling the state broadcaster Rossia 24 that it was important Trump "started talking about how America is sick and that the problems of American society need to be addressed" during his victory speech.[n] Separately she wrote on Telegram, "Those who win are the ones who live with love for their own country, not with hatred toward others."[n] Taken together, the two officials' remarks were read as Moscow adopting a cautious wait-and-see approach to the incoming administration.[n]

title: Congratulating Trump on the 2024 election
body: Netanyahu was the first world leader to congratulate [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] on his November 2024 election victory, posting on social media: "Dear Donald and Melania Trump, Congratulations on history's greatest comeback!"[n] He added that Trump's "historic return to the White House offers a new beginning for America and a powerful recommitment to the great alliance between Israel and America."[n] The message came as Israel remained at war with Hamas and Hezbollah following the October 7, 2023 attack, described in reporting on the congratulations as the deadliest single-day antisemitic attack since the Holocaust.[n]

title: Congratulating Trump on the 2024 election
body: Von der Leyen congratulated [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] on his November 2024 election victory in a social media post, writing: "I warmly congratulate Donald J. Trump. The EU and the US are more than just allies. We are bound by a true partnership between our people, uniting 800 million citizens. So let's work together on a strong transatlantic agenda that keeps delivering for them."[n] Badlands commentary read the rush of European congratulations as the "submission grins" of a fading globalist bloc, noting that Trump had simultaneously threatened tariffs marking up EU goods by 100–200 percent.[n]

title: Congratulating Trump on the 2024 election
body: Starmer, the Labour prime minister of the United Kingdom, congratulated [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] on a "historic election victory" in November 2024, posting on X: "As the closest of allies, we stand shoulder to shoulder in defense of our shared values of freedom, democracy and enterprise. From growth and security to innovation and tech, I know that the UK-US special relationship will continue to prosper on both sides of the Atlantic for years to come."[n] Badlands writer [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] grouped Starmer with Emmanuel Macron and the Brussels institutions among the world leaders lining up to pay respects to the president-elect.[n]

title: Congratulating Trump on the 2024 election
body: Zelenskyy congratulated [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] on his November 2024 election victory, despite Trump having repeatedly called for a negotiated resolution to the war between Ukraine and Russia.[n] Badlands writer [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] characterized him dismissively as the "Proxy Prince in Ukraine" among the procession of leaders offering congratulations to the president-elect.[n]

title: Lame-duck push for a Saudi security agreement
body:
Before leaving office in January 2025, Biden sought to sign a bilateral security agreement with Saudi Arabia, according to reporting by Axios journalist [[barak-ravid|Barak Ravid]] in November 2024, after his administration failed to broker a normalization deal between Israel and the kingdom.[n] The contemplated arrangement fell short of the full defense treaty the two governments had earlier discussed, but Crown Prince [[mohammed-bin-salman|Mohammed bin Salman]] and the White House still wanted a security agreement concluded before the transition.[n] The effort sat awkwardly against Biden's 2020 campaign platform of holding the Gulf kingdom responsible for the killing of Washington Post journalist [[jamal-khashoggi|Jamal Khashoggi]] and for the Saudi-led war in Yemen, which claimed roughly 400,000 lives; the administration announced some restrictions on weapons sales that were later lifted, while top officials worked to expand the Trump-era [[abraham-accords|Abraham Accords]] to include Riyadh.[n] Badlands writer [[ghostofbasedpatrickhenry|GhostofBasedPatrickHenry]] argued that the shot clock had run out on the initiative and that the incoming Trump administration, not Biden, would claim any Middle East peace breakthrough.[n]

Biden's 81 million votes in 2020 also featured prominently in Badlands analysis of the 2024 result, with commentators contrasting that figure against Barack Obama's 69 million in 2008 and 65 million in 2012, Hillary Clinton's 65 million in 2016 and [[kamala-harris|Kamala Harris]]'s roughly 66 million in 2024 to argue that some 15 million votes had appeared only once, in November 2020.[n]

title: Reporting on a US–Saudi security agreement (2024)
body: In November 2024, Ravid reported for Axios that the United States and Saudi Arabia were discussing a possible security agreement that would not involve a broader deal with Israel — a step back from the full defense treaty previously under negotiation, but one that Crown Prince [[mohammed-bin-salman|Mohammed bin Salman]] and the White House hoped to conclude before [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]] left office in January 2025.[n] Badlands writer [[ghostofbasedpatrickhenry|GhostofBasedPatrickHenry]] noted that [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] regularly uses Ravid for interviews and to deploy his own narratives inside Israel, and treated the report as a narrative that had been "cooking for quite some time" without thawing.[n]

title: US security agreement talks and the 2024 transition
body: In November 2024, Axios reported that the crown prince and the [[joe-biden|Biden]] White House were pursuing a bilateral US–Saudi security agreement — narrower than the full defense treaty once contemplated — that they hoped to conclude before the presidential transition in January 2025, after efforts to pair it with Israeli–Saudi normalization collapsed.[n] Badlands writer [[ghostofbasedpatrickhenry|GhostofBasedPatrickHenry]] framed the push as the [[deep-state|Deep State]] belatedly courting MBS, arguing that the crown prince was instead "absolutely giddy" at [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s return and had already demonstrated independence by holding joint naval drills with Iran while Washington agitated toward confrontation with Tehran.[n]

title: Wind-down of the federal cases after the 2024 election
body: Following [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s victory in the November 2024 election, Justice Department officials moved to "wind down" the two federal criminal cases Smith had brought — one over alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election, the other over the alleged mishandling of classified documents — in order to comply with department policy against prosecuting a sitting president.[n] NBC News reported that the department saw no avenue to hold trials before Inauguration Day in January 2025, particularly given the many appellate opportunities available to Trump's legal team that could reach the Supreme Court.[n] The policy against prosecuting a sitting president had been developed in the wake of Watergate and functioned as a hard deadline.[n] Smith's prosecutors had carried out a flurry of pre-election activity, filing a retooled case arguing the merits of the charges in light of the Supreme Court's presidential-immunity ruling and a rebuttal to Trump's claim that Smith's appointment was unconstitutional.[n]

title: Message to Trump after the 2024 election
body: Days after [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s November 2024 election victory, a source within Ansar Allah told Newsweek that the president-elect could avoid further damage to the US economy by reining in Israel's war in the Gaza Strip.[n] The group had begun launching missiles and drones at Israel weeks after the October 2023 Hamas attack and then turned to targeting commercial vessels accused of Israeli ties, producing a steep decline in traffic through the Suez Canal and soaring global trade costs.[n] Ansar Allah vowed to continue the campaign despite US and Israeli strikes on Yemen, tying any halt to an end of Israeli operations in Gaza and Lebanon.[n] The source expressed skepticism that Trump would deliver: "We believe that Trump will not fulfill his commitment to Arab voters and supporters of Gaza, whom he promised to stop the aggression on Gaza, but reality will answer that."[n] He added that "America is paying an economic and military price because of its support for the aggression on Gaza and also because of its aggression on Yemen in service of Israel," and asked whether continued American aggression would mean further losses for the US economy.[n]

title: Post-2024 election commentary
body: After [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] won both the Electoral College and the national popular vote in November 2024, Badlands writer [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] noted the irony that Colorado had "passed" the compact in 2020, meaning that once in effect the state's electors would be bound to the national popular-vote winner regardless of how Colorado voted.[n] She stressed that the compact was not yet operative, since it takes effect only when participating states reach 270 or more electoral votes and the signatories then stood at 209.[n] Ashe further argued that the compact violates the Twelfth Amendment to the US Constitution and should be dead on arrival.[n]

title: Winding down the Trump prosecutions (November 2024)
body: In the days after the November 2024 presidential election, Justice Department officials moved to "wind down" the two federal criminal cases against President-elect [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] brought by special counsel [[jack-smith|Jack Smith]], in order to comply with the department's post-Watergate policy against prosecuting a sitting president.[n] NBC News reported that the department saw no realistic path to holding trials before Inauguration Day in January 2025, given the appeals available to Trump's legal team and the likelihood that such appeals would reach the Supreme Court.[n]
